dam-nonneural.title: Individual differences in blood-brain barrier permeability are associated with childhood trauma and circulating immune markers in major depressive disorder: Preliminary findings.
dam-nonneural.authors: Cathomas F, Costi S, Evers A, Meyer E, Boukezzi S, Chan KL, Parise LF, Ewert J, Lun C, Xu X, Fayad ZA, Morris LS, Tang C, Russo SJ, Murrough JW.
dam-nonneural.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a major public health challenge, and childhood trauma is an important risk factor for its development. The blood-brain barrier (BBB) regulates communication between the peripheral immune system and the brain, but how childhood trauma and circulating immune alterations relate to BBB permeability in MDD remains unclear. We studied 39 participants with MDD and 22 healthy controls (HC). Childhood trauma was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ), BBB permeability was measured using dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and circulating leukocyte subtypes and immune-related proteins were quantified in blood. Covariate-adjusted linear models accounted for age, gender, body mass index, race, ethnicity, and current psychiatric medication where applicable. Blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability did not differ significantly between participants with MDD and HC. Within the MDD group, higher whole-brain BBB permeability was associated with greater childhood trauma, specifically higher CTQ total, emotional abuse, and physical abuse scores, as well as higher circulating monocyte and neutrophil counts. In a hypothesis-driven analysis based on our prior work, higher plasma matrix metalloproteinase 8 (MMP8) was associated with higher BBB permeability. In an exploratory Olink screen, fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) was the only protein associated with whole-brain BBB permeability after correction for multiple testing, with higher FGF21 related to lower permeability. The corresponding whole-brain associations were not significant in HC. Our preliminary findings identify dimensional associations of BBB permeability with childhood trauma and circulating immune measures within MDD, without evidence of a disorder-level increase in BBB permeability. They support further investigation of the BBB as a potential interface linking childhood adversity and peripheral immune processes in depression, while requiring replication in larger longitudinal samples.
